units.translation: 281. μάτην ἀράβη〈σαν〉: expecting always, because they were very close, both to bite and to touch [seem].
282-83a. μάλα σχεδόν: rushing near the Harpies. Lg (P)
b. ἐπέχραον ἤλιϑα χερ〈σί〉: often, he says, having wished to strike them, they brought their hands in vain.

285. ἐπὶ Πλωτῇσι: to the islands that are sailed around and washed on all sides by the waves; he means the Strophades islands. And other poets also say that the Harpies were overtaken at the Plotae, which are now called Strophades. These islands are in the Sicilian sea. 〈...〉 which the poet says (B 677) 'and the islands Calydnae'.
286. εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὠκέα Ἶρις: others say it was Hermes. And cleverly he assigns to this goddess the stopping of the Boreads, either because she is a messenger or because she is the sister of the Harpies.
292. ὀπιδνοτάτη: honored and worthy of regard, from ὄπις and regard, because she punishes the perjured. And ῥιγίστη means shuddering.

296-97a. Στροφάδας δέ: he says they are called Strophades because the Boreads turned back from there, having turned around, taking this from Antimachus (fg 13 B. II 291). But others say they are called Strophades because, having turned around there, they prayed to Zeus 〈for the〉 catching
of the Harpies. But according to Hesiod (fg 59 Rz.²) and Antimachus (see above) and Apollonius they are not killed.

b. πάρος Πλωτὰς καλέοντ〈ες〉: the Plotae islands were renamed Strophades. Antimachus also mentions them in the Lyde (see sch. a). 〈...〉. And that Zetes and his companions, having turned, prayed to Zeus, Hesiod also says (fg 57 Rz.²): 'there they prayed to Aenian Zeus who rules on high.' For Aenus is a mountain of Cephallenia, where there is a sanctuary of Zeus Aenesius, which Cleon mentions in his Periplus (M. IV 365) and Timosthenes in his Harbors (fg 39 E. A. Wagner Die Erdbeschreibung des T., Diss. Lips. 1888, 72). Apollonius, then, says that Iris turned back Zetes and his companions, but Hesiod (fg 58 Rz.²) says Hermes. The Plotae islands lie in the Sicilian sea.

299. κευϑμῶνα Κρήτης: they sank into a hollow of Crete. Neoptolemus also says this. And the author of the Naupactica (fg 3 Kink.) and Pherecydes in book 6 (3 fg 29 J.) say that they fled into the cave of Crete under the hill Arginus.
b. φοιβήσαντες: having cleansed the dirty body. For he said (v. 200) 'his skin was parched with dirt', he was dried up with filth.
So φοιβήσαντες means having made bright, having cleansed; for φοῖβος means pure, whence also Phoebus Apollo, because of purity.
c. ἐπικριδόν: having chosen, they sacrificed. Lg (P)
